name: The Turul
summary: A great mythical falcon came to Emese in a dream, and a river of light flowed from her. Her son Álmos began the line of Árpád, who led the Magyars into the Carpathian Basin.
fact: A giant bronze turul spreads its wings over Buda Castle, and the bird is still on Hungarian military emblems.

name: The Wondrous Stag
where: Shores of the Sea of Azov
firstText: Simon of Kéza, Gesta Hunnorum et Hungarorum (around 1283)
summary: The brothers Hunor and Magor chased a shining white stag into the marshes, where it vanished. There they found new lands and wives, and became the ancestors of the Huns and the Magyars.
fact: The Csodaszarvas legend is why so many Hungarian songs, coats of arms and folk-art pieces show a stag with stars in its antlers.

name: The Táltos
summary: A táltos was born with teeth or an extra finger. In trance they flew to the sky as bulls or stallions to fight other táltos for good weather, and could heal and find hidden things.
fact: Some people accused of witchcraft in Hungary told their judges proudly that they were táltos who protected the harvest.

name: The Lidérc
summary: Hatch the egg of a black hen under your armpit and you get a lidérc: a little demon that brings you gold, then demands endless work, or visits at night as a fiery lover and drains your strength.
fact: The only way to get rid of one was to give it impossible tasks, like carrying water in a sieve.

name: Tündér Ilona
summary: Fairy Ilona, queen of the fairies, loves Prince Árgirus. Each night her fairies steal golden apples from his father's tree, until the prince stays awake to catch them.
fact: Hungarian place names like Tündérkert ('fairy garden') come from this tradition.

name: The Garabonciás
firstText: Hungarian folk belief recorded in the 1700s
summary: A wandering 'student' with a magic book who begs for milk and eggs. Refuse him, and he rides a dragon out of a lake and calls down hailstorms on your village.
fact: The name may come from 'grammaticus', a scholar, from a time when educated wanderers seemed half-magical.

name: The Blood Countess
summary: Countess Erzsébet Báthory was arrested in 1610 and walled into her castle rooms, accused of killing many young women. Over a century later a legend appeared that she bathed in their blood to stay young.
fact: The blood-bath story is not in the 1610–1611 trial records. Historians still argue how much of the case was real and how much was politics over her vast lands.

name: The Szeged witch trials
summary: After a drought and crop failure, townspeople accused neighbours of selling the rain to the Turks. Several people, including a former town judge, were burned on an island in the river Tisza.
fact: The island is still called Boszorkánysziget, Witches' Island. Hungary's Queen Maria Theresa later banned witch trials across her lands.

name: The Serbian vampires
firstText: Report by the Habsburg official Frombald, Wienerisches Diarium (1725)
summary: In 1725 villagers of Kisiljevo said the dead peasant Petar Blagojević was rising at night and strangling people. Officials watched the grave being opened and staked. In 1732 a report on Arnaut Pavle of Medveđa made vampires famous across Europe.
fact: The word 'vampire' entered German, English and French through these newspaper reports from Serbia.

name: The Upir
firstText: A Novgorod manuscript copied by a priest who signed himself 'Upir Lichy' (1047)
summary: The upir or upyr is the oldest Slavic name for the restless dead who drink the life of the living. Medieval sermons warned people not to make offerings to them.
fact: The earliest written trace is a joke-like signature: a priest calling himself 'Upir the Wicked' in 1047.

name: The revenant of Blau
firstText: Chronicle of Abbot Neplach of Opatovice (written 1360s)
summary: In 1336, a dead herdsman named Myslata was said to rise from his grave, call out villagers' names, and those he called died. He was staked, but laughed that it only gave him a stick to fight dogs. In the end they burned him.
fact: It is one of the earliest written vampire-like stories in Europe, nearly 400 years before the Serbian cases.

name: The Golem of Prague
summary: Rabbi Judah Loew made a giant of river clay and brought it to life with a holy word to defend Prague's Jewish quarter. When it grew too strong, he took the word away and it fell back to dust.
fact: The rabbi was real (he died in 1609), but the golem story was attached to him over two centuries later. Legend says it still lies in the attic of the Old-New Synagogue.

name: Master Hanuš and the Prague clock
firstText: Prague tradition, written down from the 1500s
summary: The city councillors blinded the clockmaker so he could never build a finer clock for another city. In revenge he reached into the mechanism and stopped it for years.
fact: The clock was really built in 1410 by Mikuláš of Kadaň. The cruel Hanuš story is a legend, but the clock still runs today.

name: Polednice, Lady Midday
firstText: Karel Jaromír Erben, Kytice (1853), from older folk belief
summary: In the blazing heat of noon at harvest time, a tall woman in white appears in the fields and asks hard questions. Answer wrong, or keep working, and she twists your neck or strikes you down.
fact: She may be a folk memory of sunstroke: the real danger of working through the midday heat.

name: The Vodník
firstText: Karel Jaromír Erben, Kytice (1853), from older folk belief
summary: A green-skinned water goblin with a dripping coat sits by the mill pond. He drowns the careless and keeps their souls under upturned teacups in his house beneath the water.
fact: Czech water goblins are often polite, smoke pipes and play cards with millers. Only the souls in the teacups give them away.

name: The White Lady of Rožmberk
where: Jindřichův Hradec and Český Krumlov castles
summary: The ghost of Perchta of Rožmberk (died 1476), unhappily married, walks the castles in white. White gloves mean good news; black gloves mean a death in the family.
fact: She is said to have asked for a sweet porridge to be given to the poor each year, and the custom was kept for centuries.

name: Dracula's pamphlets
summary: Vlad III of Wallachia, called the Impaler, was a real prince. German printers sold gruesome pamphlets of his cruelties, with woodcuts of him dining among impaled victims, some of the first best-selling horror stories in print.
fact: Bram Stoker borrowed the name for his vampire in 1897, but the real Vlad was never thought to be a vampire.

name: The Strigoi
summary: Troubled souls who rise from the grave and visit their families, drawing away their strength. Villagers put garlic in windows and buried the suspected dead with a sickle across the neck.
fact: The name goes back to Latin 'strix', a screech owl that the Romans believed drank blood.

name: Nosferatu
firstText: Wilhelm Schmidt, an article on Romanian customs in Transylvania (1865); made famous by Emily Gerard, ‘Transylvanian Superstitions’ (1885)
summary: A name for the vampire that visitors to Transylvania wrote down in the 1800s. Emily Gerard described the nosferatu as a dead person who rises to drink the blood of the living, and wrote that only a stake through the corpse, or a pistol shot into the coffin, would stop it. Bram Stoker read her essay and gave the word to Van Helsing in Dracula (1897).
fact: Romanian villagers do not seem to have used the word. It may be a garbled ‘nesuferitul’, ‘the unbearable one’, a name for the Devil. The 1922 film Nosferatu was an unauthorised Dracula: a court ordered every copy destroyed, but a few survived.

name: The Kikimora
summary: A tiny, thin house spirit who lives behind the stove. Keep a tidy home and she helps; neglect it and she tangles your yarn, breaks dishes and sits on sleepers' chests.
fact: Hearing her spinning at night was an omen that someone in the house would soon die.

name: The Mora
summary: A night spirit that slips through the keyhole as a moth or a strand of hair and sits on your chest, so you wake unable to move or breathe.
fact: It is a folk explanation for sleep paralysis. 'Mara' is the same spirit in the English word nightmare.

name: Karakondžula
summary: During the dark days between Christmas and Epiphany, a heavy demon jumps on the backs of people out at night and rides them until the cock crows.
fact: People stayed indoors after dark during those twelve days, or carried a lantern and prayed.

name: The Vila
firstText: Serbian epic songs collected by Vuk Karadžić (from 1814)
summary: Beautiful, fierce mountain fairies who ride stags and shoot arrows. They help heroes like Prince Marko in battle, but punish anyone who steps into their dancing circles.
fact: In the epics a vila can build a city in the clouds, and she can be won as a sister-in-arms.

name: The Zmaj
firstText: Serbian epic songs collected by Vuk Karadžić (from 1814)
summary: Unlike Western dragons, the Serbian zmaj is often a protector: it fights hail-demons to save the crops and fathers great heroes.
fact: The real 15th-century despot Vuk Grgurević was nicknamed Zmaj Ognjeni Vuk, the Fiery Dragon Wolf, for his courage.

name: Baba Yaga
summary: A bony old witch who lives in a hut on chicken legs, behind a fence of skulls, and flies in a mortar steering with a pestle. Sometimes she eats children; sometimes she helps the brave.
fact: Her hut turns to face you only if you say the right words: 'Turn your back to the forest and your front to me.'

name: The Rusalka
summary: The spirit of a drowned young woman with long green hair who comes out of the river in early summer to sit in the trees, and tickles or lures young men to their death.
fact: During Rusalia week people avoided swimming and hung shirts and ribbons on birches to calm them.

name: The Wild Hunt
summary: On a winter night in 1091, the priest Walchelin saw a ghostly army pass along the road: the dead, suffering for their sins, led by a giant. Across Europe, people said a spectral hunt rode the storms.
fact: In some places the leader is Odin, in others King Arthur, Herne the Hunter, or the devil himself.

name: Krampus
summary: A hairy, horned demon with a long red tongue who walks with Saint Nicholas on 5 December, rattling chains and carrying a birch switch for naughty children.
fact: Austria's government tried to ban Krampus processions in the 1930s; today the runs are bigger than ever.

name: The Pied Piper of Hamelin
firstText: A church window in Hamelin (around 1300), now lost
summary: A piper in bright clothes rid the town of rats, but the townsfolk refused to pay. On 26 June 1284 he played again, and 130 children followed him out of town and were never seen again.
fact: Hamelin's own records date events 'from the departure of our children'. The rats were only added to the story in the 1500s.

name: The werewolf
where: Land of the Neuri (today's Belarus and Ukraine)
summary: From the Neuri who turned into wolves once a year, to Lycaon cursed by Zeus, to the werewolf trials of the 1500s, Europe has feared people who become wolves for over 2,400 years.
fact: Herodotus reported the Neuri story but added that he didn't believe it.

name: The werewolves of Ossory
summary: A priest travelling through the woods meets a wolf that speaks. It begs him to give the last rites to its dying wife: they are a man and woman of Ossory, cursed to live as wolves for seven years.
fact: This is a gentle werewolf story: the wolves are Christians, and the priest agrees.

name: Bisclavret
summary: A noble knight turns into a wolf three days a week. His wife steals his clothes so he can't change back. As a wolf he serves the king loyally, until he sees his betrayer.
fact: Marie de France was one of the first women whose poems survive in French, and she made the werewolf the hero.

name: Melusine
summary: A beautiful woman marries Count Raymond on one condition: he must never see her on Saturdays. When he spies on her bath, he sees a serpent's tail, and she flies away as a dragon.
fact: Great families from Luxembourg to the kings of Jerusalem claimed descent from her.

name: King Arthur
summary: A British war-leader who fought the Saxons in twelve battles, later grown into the king of Camelot with his knights, the sword Excalibur and the quest for the Holy Grail.
fact: In 1191 the monks of Glastonbury announced they had found Arthur's grave, which conveniently brought pilgrims and money to their burned abbey.

name: Beowulf and Grendel
summary: The monster Grendel attacks King Hrothgar's hall every night. The hero Beowulf tears off his arm, then dives into a lake to kill Grendel's even more terrible mother.
fact: The only copy of the poem was nearly lost in a library fire in 1731; its burned edges still crumble.

name: The Loch Ness Monster
summary: Saint Columba is said to have driven off a 'water beast' in the River Ness in 565. The modern monster was born in 1933, when a newspaper reported a strange creature in the loch.
fact: The famous 1934 'surgeon's photograph' was a toy submarine with a model head, as one of the hoaxers confessed in 1994.

name: The Banshee
summary: The bean sí, 'woman of the fairy mound', wails and keens outside a house before someone in an old Irish family dies.
fact: Families with an 'O' or 'Mac' name were said to have their own banshee.

name: Black Shuck
firstText: Abraham Fleming, 'A Straunge and Terrible Wunder' (pamphlet, 1577)
summary: On 4 August 1577, during a violent storm, a huge black dog burst into two churches, killing worshippers and leaving scorch marks on the door.
fact: The marks are still on the north door of Blythburgh church, and Bungay's town crest shows the dog with a lightning bolt.

name: Spring-heeled Jack
summary: A caped figure with glowing eyes who could leap over walls and breathed blue fire, attacking people in the dark lanes of Victorian London.
fact: The Lord Mayor of London announced the reports to the public in January 1838, and the newspapers ran with them for decades.

name: Selkies
summary: Seals who shed their skins to dance as people on the shore. Hide a selkie's skin, and she must stay and marry you, until the day she finds it and returns to the sea.
fact: Some Orkney families said they had selkie ancestors and webbed fingers to prove it.

name: The Kraken
summary: A sea monster so huge that sailors mistook it for an island. When it dived, the whirlpool could pull a ship down.
fact: The giant squid, the most likely real source, was only filmed alive in the deep sea in 2004.

name: The Draugr
summary: The dead who won't stay in their burial mounds: swollen, corpse-blue and impossibly strong. The ghost Glámr rides the roof of a farm at night until the hero Grettir wrestles him.
fact: To stop a draugr walking, Icelanders cut off its head and put it by its backside.

name: Fenrir
where: Iceland, where the myths were written down
summary: A wolf so huge the gods could only bind him with a magic ribbon made from the sound of a cat's footsteps and the roots of a mountain. At the end of the world he will break free and swallow Odin.
fact: The god Týr lost his hand in Fenrir's jaws as a pledge of good faith.

name: The Huldufólk
summary: The hidden people, who live in rocks and hills in a world just beside ours, with farms, churches and cows of their own.
fact: Road projects in Iceland have been rerouted around rocks said to be elf homes.

name: Medusa
summary: A Gorgon with snakes for hair whose gaze turned people to stone. The hero Perseus cut off her head while watching her reflection in his shield.
fact: Her head was used as a protective charm on shields and doorways, to scare evil away.

name: The Minotaur
summary: Half man, half bull, kept in King Minos's Labyrinth and fed young Athenians, until Theseus killed it and found his way out with Ariadne's thread.
fact: The real palace of Knossos is a maze of rooms and was full of bull imagery, which may have inspired the legend.

name: The Sirens
summary: Singers on a rocky island whose song lured sailors to their deaths. Odysseus had his men plug their ears with wax and tie him to the mast so he could listen.
fact: In early Greek art the sirens are bird-women; they only became fish-tailed mermaids in the Middle Ages.

name: Atlantis
summary: A mighty island empire that tried to conquer Athens and was swallowed by the sea in a single day and night.
fact: Plato almost certainly invented it as a moral tale, but people have searched for it from Santorini to Antarctica.

name: The Basilisk
firstText: Pliny the Elder, Natural History (77 CE)
summary: The king of serpents, whose breath withers plants and whose gaze kills. Only the weasel can defeat it.
fact: Medieval writers said a basilisk hatched from an egg laid by a cockerel and incubated by a toad.

name: Gilgamesh and Humbaba
firstText: Sumerian poems of the Ur III period (around 2100 BCE)
summary: King Gilgamesh of Uruk and his wild friend Enkidu travel to the Cedar Forest to slay its monstrous guardian Humbaba, then search for the secret of eternal life.
fact: The epic includes a great flood story with a boat and birds sent out to find land, over 1,000 years older than Genesis.

name: The Lamassu
firstText: Palace gateway statues of Ashurnasirpal II (around 880 BCE)
summary: Winged bulls or lions with human heads who guarded palace gates against chaos and evil.
fact: The statues have five legs, so they look like they're standing from the front and walking from the side.

name: The Simurgh
summary: A vast, wise bird so old it has seen the world destroyed three times. It raises the abandoned baby Zal in its nest and later saves the hero Rostam.
fact: In the poem The Conference of the Birds, thirty birds search for the Simurgh and discover that 'si murgh' means 'thirty birds': they were the Simurgh all along.

name: The Djinn
firstText: The Quran (600s), from older Arabian belief
summary: Beings made of smokeless fire, living unseen beside humans, who can be good or wicked and sometimes possess people or haunt ruins.
fact: The English word 'genie' comes from djinn, by way of a French translation of the Arabian Nights in 1704.

name: The Roc
firstText: Marco Polo's Travels (1298), and the Arabian Nights
summary: A bird so enormous it carries off elephants and drops them from a height to eat them. Sinbad ties himself to its leg to escape an island.
fact: Madagascar really had giant birds: the elephant bird, up to 3 metres tall, laid eggs bigger than footballs and died out about 1,000 years ago.

name: Ammit, the Devourer
firstText: The Book of the Dead (from around 1550 BCE)
summary: Part crocodile, part lion, part hippopotamus, she waits beside the scales where the dead person's heart is weighed against a feather. A heart heavy with sin is eaten, and the soul ceases to exist.
fact: She wasn't worshipped. She was feared, as the ultimate punishment: total oblivion.

name: The Bennu and the Phoenix
summary: The Bennu, a shining heron, was the soul of the sun god, rising from the first mound of creation. The Greeks turned it into the phoenix, which burns itself and rises from its ashes.
fact: Herodotus said the phoenix visited Egypt once every 500 years. He admitted he had only seen pictures.

name: Anansi the Spider
firstText: Recorded in West Africa and the Caribbean from the 1700s–1800s
summary: A clever spider trickster who outwits leopards, pythons and even the sky god Nyame, and wins all the world's stories for people.
fact: Enslaved Africans carried Anansi stories to Jamaica and the Americas, where he became 'Aunt Nancy' in some tellings.

name: Mami Wata
summary: A powerful water spirit, often shown as a beautiful woman with a snake around her shoulders, who brings wealth, healing and danger.
fact: She is honoured in living religious traditions from Nigeria to the Caribbean.

name: The Impundulu
summary: The lightning bird, as big as a person, whose wings beat thunder and who drops from the sky as a bolt of lightning.
fact: People said you should dig up the spot where lightning struck to find the bird's egg, which could be used for healing.

name: The Grootslang
summary: A gigantic creature, half elephant and half serpent, that lives in a bottomless cave full of diamonds and lures greedy people inside.
fact: Its cave, the 'Wonder Hole', is said to connect to the sea.

name: The Chinese dragon
summary: The lóng brings rain, rules rivers and seas, and is a symbol of luck and imperial power, nothing like the treasure-hoarding dragons of Europe.
fact: Jade dragon-like 'pig-dragons' from the Hongshan culture are over 5,000 years old.

name: The Nian
firstText: Chinese New Year tradition, recorded in the 1900s
summary: A beast that came out of the sea or mountains every New Year's Eve to eat crops and children, until people learned it feared loud noises, fire and the colour red.
fact: It's the story told to explain firecrackers and red decorations at Chinese New Year.

name: The Jiangshi
firstText: Yuan Mei's ghost stories (1788) and Ji Yun's notes (1790s)
summary: A stiff corpse that hops with arms outstretched, drawing the life force from the living. A paper charm stuck on its forehead stops it.
fact: The legend may come from 'corpse walkers' who carried the dead home over mountain paths on bamboo poles at night, so the bodies seemed to bounce.

name: Kitsune
summary: Fox spirits that grow a new tail every hundred years, up to nine. They can take human form, often as beautiful women, and can be faithful messengers of the god Inari or wicked tricksters.
fact: Thousands of stone foxes guard the shrines of Inari across Japan.

name: The Kappa
summary: A turtle-like river imp with a water-filled dish on its head. It drags swimmers into rivers, but if you bow, it bows back, spills its water and loses its strength.
fact: Kappa love cucumbers, which is why cucumber sushi rolls are called kappamaki.

name: Yuki-onna
summary: A pale woman in white who appears in snowstorms. Her icy breath freezes travellers to death, though she sometimes spares the young and beautiful.
fact: Lafcadio Hearn's 1904 version, where she marries the man she spared, made her famous worldwide.

name: The Nagas
firstText: The Mahabharata and early Buddhist texts (around 300 BCE onwards)
summary: Divine serpent beings who live in jewelled underwater palaces, guard treasures and the waters, and can take human form. The naga king Mucalinda sheltered the Buddha from a storm.
fact: Nagas are honoured in living Hindu and Buddhist traditions; many-headed naga balustrades line the bridges of Angkor.

name: The Rakshasas
summary: Shape-shifting demons who haunt cremation grounds and disturb holy men. Their ten-headed king Ravana kidnapped Sita, sparking the great war of the Ramayana.
fact: Every year at Dussehra, giant effigies of Ravana are burned across India.

name: The Aswang
firstText: Juan de Plasencia, Spanish friar's account (1589)
summary: A shape-shifter who looks like an ordinary neighbour by day and at night becomes a beast or a flying horror that hunts the sick and the unborn.
fact: Rumours of aswang in Capiz were so strong that it was long a joke in the Philippines that the province was full of them.

name: Taniwha
firstText: Recorded in the 1800s, from far older Māori tradition
summary: Powerful beings who live in rivers, lakes and the sea. Many are guardians of particular tribes; others are dangerous.
fact: Taniwha are part of living Māori belief, and road and building projects in New Zealand have been changed out of respect for them.

name: The Rainbow Serpent
firstText: Rock art in Arnhem Land (possibly 6,000 years old)
summary: A great creator serpent known to many Aboriginal peoples by many names, who shaped rivers, waterholes and the land, and who controls water, life and the law.
fact: These are sacred stories that belong to their peoples, and some parts may only be told by the right people. Learn them from Aboriginal sources and storytellers.

name: The Bunyip
summary: A terrifying creature said to lurk in swamps, creeks and billabongs, bellowing at night and dragging animals and people into the water.
fact: In 1845 the Geelong Advertiser reported that a fossil bone had been identified as a bunyip's. The word comes from the Wathaurong language of the Geelong area.

name: The Yowie
summary: A huge, hairy ape-man said to roam the bush of eastern Australia, Australia's answer to Bigfoot.
fact: Colonial newspapers called it the 'hairy man'; the name yowie only became popular in the 1970s.

name: The Min Min lights
summary: Glowing balls of light that follow travellers across the outback at night, then vanish when approached.
fact: A neuroscientist suggested in 2003 that they may be a desert mirage that bends the light of distant headlights or campfires.

name: Bigfoot and Sasquatch
firstText: J. W. Burns, Maclean's magazine (1929), and the Humboldt Times (1958)
summary: A giant, hairy forest-dweller of the Pacific Northwest, said to leave huge footprints in the mud.
fact: 'Sasquatch' comes from the Halkomelem word sásq'ets. The name Bigfoot came from a 1958 newspaper story about giant tracks at a logging site, which the family of a worker later said he had faked with carved feet.

name: La Llorona
summary: A weeping woman in white who wanders by rivers at night crying for her drowned children. Children are warned not to stay out after dark, or she will take them.
fact: Sahagún's Aztec informants described a woman heard crying at night, 'my children, we must flee', as one of the omens before the Spanish conquest.

name: Quetzalcoatl
firstText: Temple of the Feathered Serpent, Teotihuacan (around 200 CE)
summary: The Feathered Serpent, a god of wind, learning and creation, who in Aztec myth helped make humanity from the bones of an earlier world.
fact: The story that the Aztecs mistook Cortés for Quetzalcoatl returning was probably invented after the conquest.

name: El Dorado
summary: A Muisca ruler, covered in gold dust, rode a raft onto a sacred lake and threw gold offerings into the water. The Spanish turned the 'gilded man' into a whole lost city of gold.
fact: In 1969 a solid-gold Muisca raft showing exactly this ceremony was found in a cave near Bogotá.

name: Curupira
firstText: Letter of the missionary José de Anchieta (1560)
summary: A forest guardian with flaming red hair and feet that point backwards, so hunters who follow his tracks walk the wrong way and get lost.
fact: Anchieta, who wrote the first grammar of Old Tupi, reported that people left offerings for him on forest paths.

name: El Chupacabra
summary: The 'goat-sucker', a spiny creature blamed for killing farm animals and draining their blood.
fact: The witness behind the first famous description had just watched the alien film Species, and the creature looked remarkably like it.

name: The Mothman
summary: A tall winged figure with glowing red eyes seen near an old explosives factory, a year before the town's Silver Bridge collapsed.
fact: Point Pleasant now holds a Mothman Festival and has a shiny metal Mothman statue.

name: The Headless Horseman
firstText: Washington Irving, The Legend of Sleepy Hollow (1820)
summary: The ghost of a soldier who lost his head to a cannonball rides at night searching for it, and chases the schoolmaster Ichabod Crane.
fact: Headless riders were common in Irish and German folklore long before Irving, like the Irish Dullahan.

name: The Flying Dutchman
summary: A ghost ship doomed to sail forever around the Cape of Good Hope. Seeing it glow in a storm is an omen of disaster.
fact: In 1881 the future King George V recorded seeing it from HMS Bacchante; the sailor who first spotted it fell from the rigging and died soon after.

name: Leviathan
summary: A twisting sea serpent of chaos, defeated by the storm god in Canaanite myth and by God in the Book of Job.
fact: Thomas Hobbes named his 1651 book about the power of the state after it.

name: The Yeti
firstText: B. H. Hodgson, Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal (1832)
summary: A large ape-like being of the high snows, part of Sherpa and Tibetan belief long before Western climbers heard of it.
fact: The name 'Abominable Snowman' came from a mistranslation in a 1921 newspaper report about Everest climbers.

name: The Witch of Grič (Grička vještica)
where: Grič (Gradec), the old upper town of Zagreb
firstText: Marija Jurić Zagorka, Grička vještica (novels, from 1912), drawing on Zagreb's witch-trial records
summary: In Zagorka's novels the 'Witch of Grič' is the brave Countess Nera, whom her enemies brand a witch while she fights the witch-hunts of 18th-century Zagreb. Behind the story lie real trials on Grič hill, where women accused of witchcraft were tortured, and some burned.
fact: Croatia's last witch trial was in 1758: Empress Maria Theresa stopped the case of Magdalena Logomer, called Herucina, and she was set free. Zagorka was Croatia's first woman professional journalist.

name: The Hammer of Witches
firstText: Heinrich Kramer, Malleus Maleficarum, printed at Speyer (1486)
summary: The Dominican inquisitor Heinrich Kramer wrote a handbook on how to find, question and punish witches, claiming they were mostly women in league with the Devil. Printing presses spread it across Europe in many editions.
fact: Kramer wrote it after a failed witch trial in Innsbruck in 1485, where the local bishop threw him out of the city.

name: The Benandanti
firstText: Records of the Inquisition at Udine and Cividale (from 1575)
summary: People born with the caul, the 'good walkers', said that on certain nights their spirits left their bodies to fight witches in the fields, armed with fennel stalks against the witches' sorghum, so that the harvest would be good.
fact: The inquisitors could not understand them at first. Over decades they pushed the benandanti to confess that they themselves were witches.

name: The North Berwick witches
summary: When storms nearly wrecked King James VI's ship as he brought his bride home from Denmark, more than seventy people were accused of raising the storms by witchcraft, at a gathering in North Berwick's kirk.
fact: The king questioned some of the accused himself, and in 1597 he published his own book on witches, Daemonologie.

name: The witches of Zugarramurdi
firstText: Records of the auto-da-fé at Logroño (1610)
summary: Villagers were accused of meeting the Devil, the 'akelarre', in a cave near the French border. At Logroño in 1610 eleven people were condemned; six were burned, and five who had died in prison were burned in effigy.
fact: Afterwards the inquisitor Alonso de Salazar Frías investigated and found no real evidence of witchcraft. After that the Spanish Inquisition burned almost no witches.

name: The Pendle witches
firstText: Thomas Potts, The Wonderfull Discoverie of Witches in the Countie of Lancaster (1613)
summary: Two feuding families living around Pendle Hill accused each other of witchcraft. At Lancaster in 1612, ten people were found guilty and hanged; much of the evidence came from a nine-year-old girl, Jennet Device.
fact: About twenty years later, in 1634, Jennet Device herself was accused of witchcraft.

name: The Vardø witch trials
summary: After a storm on Christmas Eve 1617 drowned about forty fishermen, women were accused of raising it by witchcraft. Over the following decades about ninety people, many of them Sámi, were executed in Finnmark.
fact: Since 2011 the Steilneset Memorial at Vardø, by the artist Louise Bourgeois and the architect Peter Zumthor, remembers each victim by name.

name: The Bamberg witch trials
firstText: Trial records, and Johannes Junius's letter to his daughter (1628)
summary: Between 1626 and 1631 the Prince-Bishop of Bamberg built a special witch prison, the Drudenhaus, and hundreds of people were tortured into confessing and then executed.
fact: The town's mayor, Johannes Junius, smuggled a letter to his daughter before he died, explaining that he was innocent and had confessed only under torture. It still survives.

name: Walpurgis Night on the Brocken
summary: On the night before the first of May, witches were said to fly on brooms and goats to the top of the Brocken, the highest peak in northern Germany, to dance with the Devil.
fact: Goethe set a famous Walpurgis Night scene on the Brocken in Faust (1808). Today the Harz towns celebrate it with witch costumes and bonfires.

name: The Salem witch trials
firstText: Court records, and Cotton Mather, Wonders of the Invisible World (1693)
summary: In 1692 young girls in Salem Village began to have fits and accused neighbours of bewitching them. More than two hundred people were accused; nineteen were hanged, and Giles Corey was pressed to death under stones.
fact: The very last of the condemned, Elizabeth Johnson Jr., was officially cleared by the state of Massachusetts in 2022, 329 years later.

name: The Bell Witch
firstText: Martin Van Buren Ingram, An Authenticated History of the Famous Bell Witch (1894)
summary: From 1817 the Bell family's farm was said to be haunted by an invisible spirit that knocked, sang, slapped the children and talked. It tormented John Bell above all, and he died in 1820.
fact: Local tradition says General Andrew Jackson came to see the witch for himself, but no record from the time shows that he did.
